review_basis: Visually inspected all 23 original numbered Module 11 WebP slides directly, including actual titles, diagram arrows, labels, examples, numbers and caveats. Topic-first groups reflect this verified image order.
part_title: Responsibility Scope, Governed ML Lifecycle and MLOps

scenes.title: Generative AI Security Scoping Matrix
scenes.narration: The five columns show how your responsibilities generally grow as you move from using AI to building it. A public consumer chat app means you mostly follow safe-use and data-sharing policies; it is usually outside your AWS account. With enterprise AI such as Amazon Q Business, your organization also configures users, access and sharing. Building an application on a pretrained model through Bedrock adds ownership of prompts, retrieval data, tools, API access and application safeguards, even though AWS operates managed hosting. Fine-tuning brings new obligations for training datasets, customization, evaluation and deployment. Training a model from scratch adds the greatest direct responsibility for the training process and model risk. The bottom horizontal bar reminds us that privacy, identity, governance, residency and logging apply at every scope, not only the final one. The key exam question is: what exactly has the customer built, configured or trained?

scenes.title: ML Lifecycle Through Governance
scenes.narration: Follow the seven stages from left to right, beginning with a business problem and measurable success criteria. Next, frame it as classification, regression or forecasting, then prepare trustworthy data and useful features. Train and tune a model, evaluate its performance and fairness against business goals, and only then deploy and monitor it. Retraining becomes appropriate when new data or deteriorating performance makes the current model unsuitable. Notice the three gold governance gates beneath the arrows. The data gate checks provenance, privacy and bias before training. The evaluation gate checks business fit, explainability and risk before release. The deployment gate requires production-readiness review, approval and monitoring ownership. The lower loan-approval example ties those gates to a real business decision with risk controls. Governance is not a final compliance stamp: it is a series of accountable decisions throughout the model lifecycle.

scenes.title: MLOps
scenes.narration: MLOps means applying repeatable software-engineering practices to machine learning so teams can version, test, deploy and monitor models reliably. The five panels start with versioning data in S3, source code in a repository and model metadata in the SageMaker registry. Next, build and training jobs run tests and evaluate model quality. A delivery pipeline can move an approved candidate through staging and into production. CloudWatch then checks operational health, while SageMaker Model Monitor can detect configured data or model-quality deviations. The last panel is essential: the model registry records approval status and provides a path back to a previous approved version. In the fraud-detection example, new transactions lead to a tested model, not an automatic replacement. Detecting drift does not by itself retrain or deploy anything; the team must configure triggering, tests and approval. Note that the diagram uses CodeCommit as a code-repository example; the general MLOps principle does not depend on that particular source-control product.

scenes.title: MLOps Reference Architecture
scenes.narration: This is the previous slide expanded into an end-to-end AWS architecture. Follow the four numbered stages. Data arrives in S3, is prepared with Glue and can be queried through Athena for inspection. SageMaker trains and evaluates models, and pipeline tooling coordinates reproducible builds and tests. The diamond is an approval gate: a candidate model should not advance just because training finished. SageMaker Model Registry maintains versions and approval status, and SageMaker endpoints can serve real-time predictions; batch transformation is a separate mode that does not require a persistent endpoint. Finally, CloudWatch monitors service signals and SageMaker Model Monitor can flag configured drift or quality changes. The return arrow represents an orchestrated feedback process. A CloudWatch alarm, EventBridge rule or Lambda workflow must actually be configured to initiate evaluation or retraining; the slide does not imply automatic retraining by default. The bottom row distinguishes data, code and model repositories. In the fraud example, those versioned artifacts make a new model auditable and allow a controlled rollback if the production result is worse.
